newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British Energy H1 loss narrows.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British Energy H1 loss narrows.

text.p: Nuclear power generator British Energy Plc on Thursday reported a narrower loss for the first half and predicted that electricity prices would slow in the balance of the year.

The company, posting its first results since its flotation in July, reported a pro forma pretax loss of 53 million pounds ($89 million) for the first half to September 30 compared with a loss of 169 million pounds in the year-earlier period.
The firm also said it did not expect the trend of higher prices in the market seen in the first half to continue for the rest of the year.

"The prices in the summer period have been somewhat higher, but we don't expect that to continue through the winter, half- on-half. And we expect the year-end output to be roughly the same as last year," chief executive Robert Hawley told Reuters.
He added in an interview that he hoped the firm's full-year output would be "a little bit better" than the 61.2 Terawatt hours it had last year.
British Energy's partly-paid shares slid one pence to 134.5 by 1200 GMT amid a lacklustre London stock market.

"The numbers were pretty much what we expected, perhaps a tad better," said Greig Middleton analyst David Campbell, adding that he did not expect the outlook for short-term electricity prices to hurt the company's stock.

"It's had an extremely good run, and we would anticipate possibly a bit of a pause for breath. I wouldn't be surprised if after market consideration (of the results), the share price continues to go ahead," he said.
The shares were currently outperforming the Financial Times All-Share Index by about 36 percent and the company's sector by roughly 27 percent, according to Reuters Securities 3000 data.
British Energy said its output surged 12 percent to 31.5 Terawatt hours in the first half, boosted by maintenanence outages at its competitors' plants.
A Terawatt hour, the largest unit of measurement for electricity sales, represents one billion kilowatt hours.
Meanwhile, net operating cash flow surged to 140 million pounds from 54 million.
The firm also said it agreed to supply electricity to Southern Electric Plc for up to 15 years, expanding the companies' existing relationship.
Hawley declined to give financial details, but he did say the deal would increase British Energy's sales to Southern, which amounted to 6.5 Terawatt hours last year.
"What we're looking at now is a situation where it will be somewhat north of that for a period of 15 years," Hawley said.
"And of course from our point of view, the advantage is it gives us a degree of longer-term price stability which hedges against the uncertainty in pool prices," he added.
Hawley said British Energy was talking to other electricity companies about similar deals.
He added the company was focusing on increasing output and cost-savings at its existing power stations but would also consider joint ventures in the UK and investments overseas.
British Energy set an interim dividend of 4.6p per share, in line with its previous estimates.
"If the wind's in the right direction, and all sorts of things, we are pretty confident we'll meet our final dividend of 13.7p. That's exactly spot-on with what was in the prospectus," Hawley said.
